name: PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Karya Pacific Energy — a quota-bound coal ramp at a discount
frontmatter.summary: IATA trades at Rp72 against our Rp113 target — BUY, 57.1% expected return — on a valuation correction, not an operating one: the non-operating licences are carried at book value, the trough multiple's weight is cut, the statutory tax rate replaces a one-year benefit and a weighted dilution cost sits inside the target. The FX fix is disclosure, not a value driver. At the market price the deck's benchmark is discounted, not exceeded.
thesis: The shares have fallen well below our value after the third-quarter report: nine-month net profit attributable to shareholders was US$1.0m against US$7.2m a year earlier, on flat revenue, a US$2.4m exchange loss and higher finance costs [S16, S17]. The operating ramp is intact on the nine months' revenue and the signed KPP contract, not on a quarter-on-quarter profit gain: the third quarter's gross profit — the nine-month US$21.7m less the first-half US$12.1m — came in below the first half's total, though above the half's per-quarter run-rate. We therefore cut neither volume nor price. The previous revision's ADD rested on an uncited spot; the engine now reads the macro deck's USD/IDR spot by id — disclosed, and inconsistent with the deck's own basis note — and the last onshore print we can cite is Rp18,080/USD on 23 October [S19]. The target is Rp113 and the return 57.1%, so the rating is BUY; the lift in value comes from carrying the unvalued licences and reweighting the trough multiple, not from the FX citation or a more bullish operating case.

The volume ramp is real — a five-year KPP Mining contract and a 298 Mt reserve base support a move toward 7.0 Mt — but the cash economics are thin: even at US$30.4m of EBITDA, US$7.5m of capex, tax and working capital leave only US$12.2m of FCFF.

The product is low-calorie thermal coal priced off HBA III [S8], not the 6,000 kcal Newcastle benchmark: the war-premium Newcastle tape does not flow through to IATA's realised price, and the company's own HBA III estimate for 2026 is below the 2025 average [S8 p.86].

Liquidity remains tight: nine-month cash fell to US$1.5m while inventories rose to US$37.5m, factoring liabilities rose to US$8.1m, and third-quarter current liabilities topped current assets, as the company navigates the Series B refinancing [S16, S17].

The controller acquired 663.2 million shares at an exercise price of Rp87.0 in October, raising the stake to 62.5%, but that is a pre-agreed scheme price rather than an open-market purchase and does not improve the free float or supply a liquidity solution [S16]. The rating is BUY because the operating value sits well above the market price; the small float is an investability constraint, not a reason to mark the shares up to their value today.

blocks.text: **The tape and the whisker: the same fall, served a third time — and this time the honest answer is that the valuation moved, not the company.** This is the third consecutive queue item built on one unexplained decline in the shares, and the archive has not moved: the last dated mark in the data pack is still Rp72 [S0], the last company filing is the 30 September LK [S17], and nothing archived after 3 November supplies a cause [S16, S18]. What changed on 7 November is the valuation, and it changed a great deal: the target is Rp113 against a base value of Rp119 and a raw DCF of Rp115 — about a fifth above the level published on 6 November — and the drivers are corrections this review forced, none of which is a more bullish view of coal. The value comes from two lines and is partly given back by two others. First, the three non-operating IUP-OPs are no longer carried at zero: they are carried at one-third of the US$77.5m mining-property and exploration carrying value [S12 p.14, Note 11], a book value that is in the filing and that the previous revision said did not exist. Second, the trough multiple's weight falls from just under a third of the blend to 15%, which raises the blend because the multiple sits far below the DCF. Against those, the tax rate steps to the 22.0% statutory rate from FY2026E, and the dilution the previous revision only described in prose is now a probability-weighted line inside the target; the two take back part of the gain. The FX fix is not a source of the restatement: the engine reads the macro deck's USD/IDR spot by id, the deck is now disclosed as the source and its spot is shown to be inconsistent with its own basis note, the last onshore print we can cite is Rp18,080/USD on 23 October [S19], and the re-mark is worth a fraction of a rupiah against the licence and reweighting lines — it is a disclosure fix, not a value driver. The net is a higher target, not a change of mind about coal. The operating case — volume, unit cost, price path — is unchanged, and the bridge from the published 6 November level, line by line with both endpoints printed, is in the assumptions file. If there is a company-specific reason for the fall, it is not in the file, and we do not invent one.

**BUY, target Rp113, 57.1% expected return.** Since our 28 October REDUCE: the shares have fallen well below our value, the third-quarter report explains why the market lost confidence — nine-month revenue of US$55.4m was flat year on year, but direct costs rose to US$33.7m, finance costs to US$4.1m, and a US$2.4m exchange loss left net profit attributable to shareholders at US$1.0m against US$7.2m a year earlier — and the previous revision removed a mechanical fuel double-count in the unit-cost line that had been understating FY2026E EBITDA and the DCF [S16, S17, S12 Note 30]. We have not cut the operating forecast: the third quarter's revenue was stronger than the first half's per-quarter run-rate, and FY2026E is now built from the nine months' actual volume, price and unit cost plus a fourth quarter at the third quarter's run-rate, not from an annual per-tonne ratio [S13, S17]. The profit collapse is below the gross-profit line — finance costs, a net exchange loss and other charges — not a failure of the volume ramp [S17]. We do not attribute the share-price fall to the market: the IHSG fell 1.1% intraday on 3 November, but a note on the index that does not mention IATA cannot explain an idiosyncratic move of this size, and we treat the fall as unexplained by the archived tape [S18]. The move is large but its timing cannot be pinned from the archive, and the packet's own tape does not agree with it. The queue item carries two dated marks — a print in the high nineties on 4 November and one in the low seventies the following day — while the data pack carries the September, October and November monthly marks with the last dated print at Rp72 on 4 November, inside a year's range of Rp54 to Rp185 [S0]. The two cannot both be right about the same session, and neither is an archived exchange record: the packet's marks are unstated as to source and the pack has no daily series. We use the archived mark and say so, because the difference is not cosmetic — if the packet is right the fall was a single-session move of about a quarter, and if the pack is right it happened between the September and November marks. Either way the magnitude is real and the dating is not established, so we do not date the move and we do not compute a five-session return from a file that holds monthly marks. The note we published on 28 October was struck at a price in the nineties of rupiah, so the fall from that note to today sits inside the same range. The two press items the previous update relied on are dated 3 November on their own pages [S16, S18], so the archive holds nothing dated after that; that establishes a gap in the file, not the absence of news, and we say so. The company — formerly PT MNC Energy Investments Tbk and now PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk — is a small South Sumatra thermal-coal producer with three operating IUP-OPs, a signed five-year mining-services contract with KPP Mining that points toward 7.0 Mt a year, and 298 Mt of stated reserves [S3, S11, S8]. Our base case delivers that ramp — FY2027E volume of 6.5 Mt — and values the equity at Rp115 per share on the DCF; the blended target is lower because the EV/EBITDA cross-check is applied to the last audited year's earnings, which are a fraction of the ramp year's, not because we shade the operating case. The product still realises a deep quality discount to HBA III, cash costs and shipping absorb most of the revenue, and the balance sheet has little room for error [S8, S12].

The variant view is not that the coal is not there. It is that IATA's cash conversion is weaker than the P&L suggests, so the equity is worth the discounted residue of a finite life of tonnes rather than a growth multiple — and, after the cost correction, that residue now sits above a price the market has taken down for reasons the archive does not record. In FY2025 the company earned US$7.6m of net profit but generated US$3.2m of operating cash flow and spent US$25.2m on fixed assets and mining properties, so net debt rose to US$52.6m [S12]. On the company's own volume plan the model reaches US$30.4m of EBITDA, but capex of US$7.5m, tax and working capital leave only US$12.2m of FCFF [S12, S8]. We have corrected the capex line so that the leased fleet is charged through the lease obligation and the cash cost rather than twice; even on that corrected basis the equity is a discounted residual, not a growth multiple.

What moves the value is narrow and identifiable. First, the low-calorie price: IATA sells 3,400 kcal/kg GAR coal, and the company's own HBA III estimate for 2026 is 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t [S8 p.86], below the 2025 HBA III average of 36.5 USD/t [S8]. The deck's reviewed mid-October HBA III print of 45.5 USD/t is above both, and it is a spot mark without a forward path; we reconcile it to the model in the valuation section rather than capitalising it across thirty years, because the method card treats spot as cycle position and never as value. Second, the RKAB quota: the 2026 national target was cut, only 2.0 Mt was approved as IATA's initial 2026 quota and the H1 revenue decline was explicitly attributed to the quota [S6, S8, S5]; the nine-month revenue implies the mid-year revision was delivered for 2026, so the live risk is whether it rolls into 2027 rather than the 2026 cap. Third, capex discipline and liquidity: the port and conveyor programme and the mining-property acquisitions are real cash calls, and the 30 September 2026 balance sheet carries inventories of US$37.5m, factoring liabilities of US$8.1m and cash of US$1.5m [S5, S12, S17].

The gap to our value is open. At Rp72 the shares trade on 12.6x EV/EBITDA and 25.0x P/E on trough FY2026E earnings, but on 5.8x and 8.6x on the FY2027E ramp year that the DCF actually values [S0]. The reverse DCF now reads the other way round from the previous revision. Measured on the deck itself, the current price requires the FY2027E Newcastle benchmark to be about eight per cent below our path, which at the FY2027E realisation of 18.0% is an implied ASP below even the FY2026E ASP of 20.8 USD/t, and an implied HBA III just under the low end of the company's own 2026 estimate [S0, S8, deck]. So the price is not assuming a better coal price than the company projects; it is assuming a modestly worse one, and discounting the mining assets to less than half the DCF's value once the non-operating bridge is set aside. The return to our blended value is 57.1%, which is why the rating is BUY rather than HOLD: the operating value sits well above the price, and the licence value and the reweighting of the trough multiple are what widened the gap, while the step to the statutory tax rate and the probability-weighted dilution cost work the other way and take a couple of points off the return. We would cut the rating on a sourced cost step-up, a contracted volume path that falls short of the plan, a refinancing at a penalty coupon, or evidence that the stockpile cannot be sold at its carried value.

IATA is a South Sumatra coal name whose history illustrates the difference between a mining licence and a mining business. The group assembled a large resource position around Musi Banyuasin, brought three concessions into production, and then had to fund the ramp through a mixture of debt, a rights issue and asset sales. The equity has always been a minority-float story: the controlling block changed hands, the free float is small, and the stock has spent time on the exchange's special monitoring board after a prolonged low price. None of that is unusual for an Indonesian small-cap coal producer, but it means the shares trade on flow and narrative as much as on discounted cash flow.

PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk is an Indonesian coal-mining group listed on the IDX under the ticker IATA. It was founded in 1968 as PT Indonesia Transport & Infrastructure Tbk, an aviation-services business, and was renamed PT MNC Energy Investments Tbk in February 2022 when it pivoted to coal [S12 Note 1]. It now operates as PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk, the name adopted after the change of controlling shareholder; the 22 June 2026 AGMS approved the FY2025 accounts and a new board, while the FY2025 annual report is still filed under the old name [S4, S6]. The group now manages six IUP-OP licences in Musi Banyuasin, South Sumatra, of which three are fully operating — PT Indonesia Batu Prima Energi (IBPE), PT Putra Muba Coal (PMC) and PT Arthaco Prima Energy (APE) [S8]. The remaining permits are at various stages of development or extension [S12 Note 1g], and the mining-property and exploration-and-evaluation line that carries them had a book value of US$77.5m at 31 December 2025 with no accumulated amortisation shown [S12 p.14, Note 11] — which is the value we allocate to the non-operating licences in the valuation section, because it is the only sourced carrying value in the file.

The revenue base is coal, with a small port-management and services line. FY2025 revenue was US$79.6m, split roughly half domestic and half export, plus a port-management fee [S12 Note 29]. The domestic leg sells into the Indonesian power and industrial market; the export leg ships low-calorie thermal coal to buyers in Asia. The customer list is concentrated: a small number of counterparties account for more than a tenth of revenue each, including PT Satria Jaya Energi, SAAI Resources and Visa Resources [S12 Note 29; S13 Note 29]. That concentration is normal for a sub-scale producer but it weakens IATA's pricing leverage and adds counterparty risk.

The operating model is contractor-led. In December 2025 IATA signed a five-year mining-services contract with PT Kalimantan Prima Persada (KPP Mining), an Astra-group contractor, covering coal getting, hauling and related work, with output targeted to rise from a lower first-year rate toward the long-run rate [S11]. The company also owns and is expanding port and conveyor infrastructure; management flagged a port and conveyor programme to support the recovery [S5]. That model lowers the company's direct labour and equipment risk but converts a large share of the cost base into contractor fees and shipping, which is why the cash-cost line is the key swing factor in the model.

Footprint and market position are modest. IATA's FY2025 production of 3.4 Mt is a small fraction of Indonesia's 790 Mt national output [S8]. It is a challenger, not a leader: it has no pricing power, no brand, no switching costs for its customers, and no control over the RKAB quota that determines how much it can sell. Its advantages are the reserve base — 298 Mt of stated reserves and 1,438 Mt of resources — and the fact that the three operating mines and the port infrastructure are already in place [S8, S12]. Those are real assets; the question for the equity is what they earn, not whether they exist.

Ownership and control changed materially in 2025-26. At 31 December 2025 PT Karya Pacific Investama held 48.8% of the shares and MNC Asia Holding held 18.8%; by October 2026 Karya Pacific Investama held 62.5%, having lifted its stake from 60.4% through the 19 October exercise of 663.2 million shares at a scheme price of Rp87.0, and the company stated it was no longer part of the MNC/Hary Tanoesoedibjo group [S12 Note 27; S4, S16]. The register is the authority on the float: the controller's 62.5% and MNC Asia's 18.8% together hold over four-fifths of the capital, leaving a residual public float of under one-fifth, and we reject the data pack's conflicting free-float field as arithmetically impossible against the insider figure it is published with [S0, S12 Note 27, S16]. The FY2025 accounts still name MNC Asia Holding as the ultimate parent and Hary Tanoesoedibjo as the ultimate beneficial owner, which is a reminder that the control transition was completed after the balance-sheet date [S12 Note 1; S4]. The new controller's strategic intentions are not disclosed in any archived source; we do not assume an asset injection.

A coal-mining group in South Sumatra typically operates through a set of concession-holding subsidiaries, with the listed parent providing the balance sheet and the permits sitting in the operating companies. The contractor model is common: a mining-services firm brings the fleet and the crews, and the concession holder pays a per-tonne or per-bcm rate. That structure can scale production quickly, but it also means the concession holder's margin is the spread between the coal price and the contractor, hauling and port costs, and it makes the cash-cost line the most important number in the investment case.

Indonesia is the world's third-largest coal producer. National output reached 790 Mt in 2025, above the RKAB target of 740 Mt, of which 254 Mt went to the domestic market and 514 Mt was exported [S8]. The government has set the 2026 RKAB target at 600 Mt, a cut, explicitly to support prices after the 2025 oversupply [S8]. That policy is the single most important industry variable for IATA: only 2.0 Mt was approved as the initial 2026 quota, the company's request for 7.8 Mt was still being processed in August, and management was pursuing a mid-year revision [S6, S8, S5]. A quota-constrained producer cannot grow faster than the regulator allows, whatever its contractor or reserve base says.

Prices are weak at the low-calorie end, which is where IATA sells. The HBA III reference for 3,400 kcal/kg GAR coal averaged US$36.5/t in 2025 and is estimated by the company at 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t for 2026; the ICI-5 index averaged US$35.2/t in 2025 and is projected in a similar range [S8]. The high-calorie HBA averaged US$111/t in 2025 and is expected lower in 2026, while the Newcastle 6,000 kcal benchmark in our coal deck is US$150/t spot and US$118/t for FY2027E, with a long-run anchor of US$105/t [S8, deck]. The spread between Newcastle and HBA III is the single best explanation of why IATA's realised price is so far below the headline thermal-coal price: it is not selling 6,000 kcal coal, and the war-premium bid for high-grade seaborne coal does not reach its product. The deck's revised HBA III print is 45.5 USD/t against a high-calorie HBA of 126.8 USD/t, a ratio of about thirty-six per cent, where the 2025 average ratio was about a third (36.5 USD/t against 111.0 USD/t) [S8, deck]. That monthly ratio is where the model has to take a position, and the valuation section sets out the one it takes. The Newcastle series is therefore only a forecastable scaling index; the HBA III realisation is the economic anchor, and the company's own 2026 estimate is the basis for our FY2026E ASP [S8].

The regulatory framework has three moving parts. The RKAB quota sets annual production and sales allowances. The domestic market obligation requires a share of output to be sold domestically, and the government has considered raising the DMO share above a quarter of production [S8]. The DHE SDA export-proceeds rule sets how much foreign-currency revenue must be retained or converted, and the government has revised the conversion limit [S8]. For IATA, the practical effect is that a larger share of revenue may be rupiah-denominated and subject to domestic price expectations, which caps the benefit of any export-price recovery. The company is an IUP-OP holder, so its royalty follows the IUP schedule rather than the IUPK schedule; the LK shows an effective royalty of 7.1% of revenue in FY2025, which is the rate we model [S12 Note 30].

Competitive positioning is weak on the five-forces test. Rivalry is high: Indonesia has hundreds of coal producers and the marginal tonne is price-taking. Buyer power is high: a handful of customers account for more than a tenth of revenue each [S12 Note 29]. Supplier power is moderate: the KPP Mining contract is a large, concentrated relationship, but it is a services contract and the contractor is replaceable in principle. Threat of entry is low for new mines because of permitting and capital, but the threat of substitution is high in the long run as renewable capacity and LNG displace thermal coal; the IEA expects global coal demand to fall from 8.8 bn t in 2025 to 8.6 bn t by 2030 [S8]. IATA has no moat beyond its licences, reserves and infrastructure, and those protect its ability to produce, not its ability to earn a return on capital.

The market-share picture is simple: IATA is a sub-one-per-cent producer in a 790 Mt national market, and its share will rise or fall with the RKAB, not with competitive wins [S8]. The company's addressable growth is therefore policy-driven. That is why the report treats the RKAB revision as a catalyst and the quota as a risk, rather than treating volume as a management execution variable.

Thermal-coal markets are cyclical and policy-sensitive, and the low-calorie end is the least defensible part of the curve. Low-rank coal is abundant, cheap to mine in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and burns at a lower efficiency, so it clears at a discount to high-grade seaborne benchmarks and is the first to be displaced when power generators can switch to gas or renewables. Indonesian producers have historically responded to price peaks by raising output, which is why the government uses RKAB quotas to manage supply. The result is a sector where the best operators earn returns through cost position and capital discipline, not through price.

IATA's reported history is a story of falling revenue and volatile margins. Revenue was US$192.1m in FY2022, US$170.1m in FY2023, US$117.9m in FY2024 and US$79.6m in FY2025 [S0]. The decline was driven by lower coal prices and a change in product quality, not by a collapse in volume: FY2024 sales were 3.7 Mt and FY2025 sales were 3.5 Mt, while FY2024 production was 4.1 Mt and FY2025 production was 3.4 Mt [S10, S8]. The audited FY2025 report [S8] governs the base volume and price, while the company's own 2025 release [S3] governs the delivery-rate benchmark used in the bear case, where the two volume sets are reconciled but not identical [S3, S8]. FY2025 revenue fell because the realised price fell faster than volume: the domestic ASP dropped and the export ASP fell to US$22.2/t [S8]. The first half of 2026 continued the pattern, with revenue of US$33.4m and net profit attributable to parent of US$1.0m [S13]; the nine months to September brought revenue of US$55.4m, essentially flat, but net profit attributable of only US$1.0m after higher direct costs, finance costs and a large exchange loss [S16, S17]. Our FY2026E revenue of US$77.4m is the nine-month actual plus a run-rate fourth quarter at 3.6 Mt, with an implied ASP of 20.8 USD/t that sits inside the company's HBA III 2026 range rather than at the Newcastle war-premium price [S8 p.86, S13, S17]. The volume is an inference and we present it as one: neither the 30 September LK nor the press report prints sales tonnage, so the nine-month figure is bounded from revenue of US$55.4m at two sourced prices — the FY2025 last-actual ASP [S8, F2] and the company's own HBA III estimate [S8 p.86] — and both bounds sit above the approved initial quota 2.0 Mt [S6, F34]. A producer cannot sell above its approved quota, so the nine-month revenue is evidence that the mid-year RKAB revision was delivered for sales purposes, even though no announcement dated after 30 September is archived; the last dated statement is management's August description of the revision as still being processed [S5]. We therefore rank the quota as a 2027 renewal risk rather than the top 2026 risk, and the FY2027E volume of 6.5 Mt rests on the signed KPP ramp rather than on an approval letter we cannot cite [S11].

The cost structure is the heart of the investment case. FY2025 direct costs were US$35.1m, of which royalties were US$5.7m and the depreciation charged in direct costs was US$2.1m; the remaining cash cost per tonne was the FY2025 rate on 3.5 Mt of sales [S12 Note 30]. The nine months to September 2026 show a materially higher rate: direct costs of US$33.7m against revenue of US$55.4m, which after the 7.1% royalty and the depreciation inside direct costs leaves a cash cost per tonne of 10.64 on the nine-month sales volume implied by that revenue at our realised price [S17]. The like-for-like comparison is against the prior-year nine months, on essentially the same revenue: direct costs rose from US$30.0m to US$33.7m, about an eighth higher, and that is the cost increase the year-on-year record supports [S17]. The rest of the gap between the nine-month rate and the FY2025 full-year rate is volume and mix, not price: the company sold less coal at a lower ASP, so the fixed component of the contractor and port cost spreads over fewer tonnes, and we state the split rather than presenting the whole level difference as a cost step-up [S17, S12 Note 30]. We carry the nine-month rate because it is the last actual. The template re-indexes a 21.0% fuel share from the FY2025 Brent price to the forecast Brent price, so the number fed into that formula is 9.8 USD/t per tonne — the FY2025-Brent equivalent of the nine-month cost, not the nine-month cost itself; charging the nine-month cost would price the 2026 fuel step twice [S12 Note 30, S17]. The engine's unit-cost line therefore prints 10.64 per tonne in FY2026E, and that is the nine-month figure to hold the equity against. Selling expenses were US$28.9m in total including operating expenses, dominated by coal shipping [S12 Notes 31/32]. That is a high cost stack for a product realising only a fraction of the HBA III marker: the model's cash margin per tonne is thin, and a small move in freight, fuel or the contractor rate moves EBITDA materially. The FY2024 cost base was even worse — subcontractor costs of US$12.2m and a different mine mix pushed the cash cost far above the FY2025 rate — which is why the FY2025 improvement is real but not yet proven through a full cycle [S12 Note 30]. Tax is now carried at the statutory rate from FY2026E. The FY2025 effective rate of 22.0% is a single-year outcome with no disclosed concession [S12 P&L]; the FY2024 rate was above the statutory rate, and the nine-month 2026 rate is distorted upward by the exchange loss, which is not deductible in the same proportion. A one-year benefit is therefore not a regime, and we apply the 22.0% statutory rate across the forecast [S12 Note 2n; S17]. That is a deliberate reduction in value against the previous revision, which held the FY2025 rate for five years and described the step as "tested in the bear" when the bear carried no tax shock.

D&A is the line where the Yahoo data pack is wrong and the LK matters. The pack's D&A line is a small fraction of the audited charge, which would imply an implausibly long asset life on a PP&E base of US$143.7m; the audited LK shows total fixed-asset depreciation of US$2.4m in FY2025 and US$2.2m in FY2024, with no mine-property amortisation charged to production in FY2025 [S12 Note 10/11]. We restate the history from the LK and carry D&A of US$0.7 per tonne in the forecast. The restatement raises EBITDA relative to a naive pack-based model, but it is the correct accounting: the depreciation is real, even though it is non-cash.

The cash-flow statement is less flattering than the P&L. FY2025 operating cash flow was US$3.2m, against net profit of US$8.3m, because working capital and tax absorbed the difference [S12 cash-flow statement]. Capex was US$25.2m, including mining-property acquisitions, so free cash flow was negative US$-27.4m [S12]. The fixed-asset part of that capex was US$12.6m [S12 Note 10]; it splits into US$4.1m of direct-ownership additions and US$8.5m of right-of-use machinery and vehicles taken under lease [S12 Note 10]. The right-of-use line is a financing of the mining fleet, not an equity cash call: the lease obligations sit inside gross debt, and the rental service cost sits in the direct-cost line the cash cost is backed out of, so adding those additions to sustaining capex would charge the same fleet twice. We therefore carry 1.16 per tonne of sustaining capex, the direct-ownership portion over FY2025 sales [F2, F43] [S12]. The company funded the gap with a rights issue and new bank borrowing; net debt ended the year at US$52.6m [S12]. That is the core of our caution: the business is not yet generating the cash needed to fund its own growth, and the equity has been the residual financier.

The balance sheet is tighter at the 30 September 2026 date. Cash was US$1.5m, inventories US$37.5m, factoring liabilities US$8.1m, current liabilities US$77.3m against current assets US$62.1m [S17]. The coal inventory alone is US$26.6m [S17 Note 8], and nine-month direct costs were US$33.7m [S17], so the stockpile is about seven months of annualised cost of sales; a quality or unsold-tonne problem would force an NRV writedown. Total liabilities rose to US$111.1m against total assets of US$242.3m, leaving equity of US$131.2m [S17]. At 31 December 2025 cash was US$2.2m against total debt of US$54.7m; the debt includes rupiah bonds whose Series B tranche reached its 6 October 2026 maturity, plus bank facilities from Mayapada and Victoria [S12 Notes 18/19/20]. The archive records neither repayment nor refinancing of the matured tranche [S12, S17]. The company has no committed undrawn facility disclosed in the archive, which is why we treat refinancing as a risk rather than a base-case assumption. We hold gross debt flat in the forecast (no net new borrowing and no repayment), which implicitly assumes the tranche is refinanced at maturity; the modelled cost of debt is the blended rate, and refinancing at a higher coupon would lower the equity value.

Capital allocation has been growth-first. The company has never paid a dividend, and the FY2025 accounts record no distribution [S0, S12]. Cash has gone into mining-property acquisitions, the APE start-up and the port/conveyor programme. Our forecast carries a zero payout — not because we think the company should never pay one, but because there is no record or policy that supports a dividend, and the capex programme has first call on cash [S12, S5]. The dividend-capacity anchor therefore does not apply to the paid stream; the valuation section discusses capacity rather than a current yield.

Earnings-quality flags, run through the house screen. The accruals ratio is modest: FY2025 net profit of US$8.3m against operating cash flow of US$3.2m on total assets of US$238.3m is a low single-digit percentage, so there is no evidence of earnings outrunning cash in the accounting sense [S12]. The bigger issue is the opposite: cash conversion is weak because capex and working capital are heavy, not because revenue is fictitious. Receivables fell with revenue. Inventory is the flag: US$37.5m at 30 September 2026, of which coal is US$26.6m [S17 Note 8], against nine-month direct costs of US$33.7m [S17]; that is about seven months of annualised cost of sales and is not a normal working stock, so an NRV writedown or an unsold-tonne/quality problem is a live risk. The nine-month result adds a second flag: the US$2.4m exchange loss and finance costs of US$4.1m together took a minority of the US$21.7m gross profit — but the bulk of operating profit — so the P&L's operating margin is a poor guide to what reaches equity [S17]. An NRV writedown would be a non-cash impairment of the stockpile: it reduces book equity and the tax shield and does not raise the cash cost per tonne, which is why we no longer model it as a per-tonne cash shock. Related-party liabilities were about six per cent of total liabilities at FY2025, mostly trade payables to PT Karya Pacific Shipping and other MNC entities, which is disclosed but worth monitoring as the control group changes [S12 Note 26]. The 2026 cash-flow statement shows US$10.3m of new related-party other-payables funding in the nine months, against 30 September cash of US$1.5m [S17 p.10, F58] — the dominant financing source in the period, and the liquidity dependence we rank in the risk section.

Two IDX regime flags need to be stated plainly. The shares entered the special monitoring board in 2024 after the average price fell below the exchange's threshold, which imposed full call auction on the stock [S15]. The September 2026 list of stocks removed from the special board does not include IATA, so the current status is unresolved in the archive and must be checked with the exchange before any position is sized [S14]. The reconciled register float is under one-fifth of the shares (the controller holds 62.5% and MNC Asia 18.8%), which magnifies the liquidity and governance risk [S12 Note 27, S16]. Neither point is a manipulation finding; both are investability constraints that belong in the risk section, not in a valuation premium.

The reported profit of a coal miner and its cash generation can diverge sharply because the P&L carries depreciation, depletion and reclamation accruals that are non-cash, while the cash-flow statement carries the capex that replaces the depleted asset. A producer can look profitable for years while consuming equity if it keeps buying mining properties and equipment. That is why a coal analysis starts with the cash-cost per tonne and the capex intensity, then tests the P&L against the cash-flow statement, rather than taking the net margin at face value.

We value IATA on a life-of-asset DCF at through-cycle prices, cross-checked against EV/EBITDA at the peer median, a dividend-capacity yield and EV/reserves. That method set fits a coal producer because the asset is finite, the price is cyclical and the P&L in any one year is a poor guide to value. We do not use a spot multiple or a current-year P/E as the primary method, because both would capitalise a single point in the coal cycle and ignore the capex and depletion that follow.

The cost of capital build is shown below. The company reports in US dollars, so the risk-free rate is the house USD government yield, the mature-market equity risk premium and the Indonesia country risk premium are house inputs, and the beta is the industry median from the house regression set, re-levered at the market-value debt-to-equity implied by the current share price. The result is a WACC of 10.6%, with a cost of equity of 13.0%. The engine's pre-tax debt cost is the house macro corporate spread (6.9%), but IATA's own rupiah debt is more expensive: the Series B and C bonds and the Mayapada/Victoria bank facilities carry double-digit rupiah coupons [S12 Notes 18/20], and the P&L's interest line is consistent with the cost of debt in the assumptions file. We add an explicit company premium of 0.8% on the cost of equity so the WACC reflects the actual debt stack; the WACC table shows it as its own line, not a hidden illiquidity premium. The premium is applied to the cost of equity and only its equity-weighted share reaches the WACC, so on the model's 31.6% debt weight and 68.4% equity weight it delivers well under its headline size — the WACC of 10.6% is a little above what the assumptions' 10.0% pre-tax debt cost would give, not fully at it. That is the one optimistic item in the model, and it is smaller than the cost correction this revision makes; the arithmetic is set out in the assumptions file. We use the market-value debt weight implied by the balance sheet and share price rather than a target mix, because the balance sheet is already levered and the DCF should reflect the financing in place.

The primary DCF is a thirty-year life model with no terminal value. The operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033 with extensions in process, so the model assumes the extension process succeeds; it runs thirty years, below the reserve life at the planned volume, and applies no terminal value because no renewal beyond the current applications is archived [S12 Note 1g; F5]. The present value is concentrated in the first decade [S12]. The DCF uses a sustaining capex of 1.16 per tonne, the FY2025 direct-ownership additions [S12 Note 10]; the right-of-use fleet additions are leases whose obligations are already in net debt and whose rental charge is already in the cash-cost line, and the mining-property acquisitions are growth, so neither is deducted again as maintenance [S12 Notes 10/11/19]. At our base assumptions the DCF produces an enterprise value of US$213.6m and an equity value of Rp115 per share after net debt and the non-operating investment bridge [S12]. The DCF is sensitive to the realised price and to capex; the sensitivity table shows the range. The model stops with 91.8 Mt of reserves still in the ground; we do not value that tail because the operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033 with extensions in process [S12 Note 1g] and a further renewal beyond the current applications is not archived. The port/conveyor programme is carried as capex with no quantified volume or cost benefit, because the archive discloses the spend but not the uplift [S5].

**The price anchor, tested — and the reconciliation to the deck's October print.** The commodity card keys Indonesian coal realisation off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle, and requires the through-cycle price to be a sourced number rather than a spot mark, because spot is cycle position and never value. The model therefore works in two steps. First, the realised price is calibrated on the last actual against its own benchmark: FY2025 revenue over FY2025 sales is a blended ASP that is 21.0% of the long-run Newcastle anchor, and that ratio — the company's own realised-to-benchmark relationship, neither a haircut nor a premium — is what the model carries into the long run [S12, F2, S8]. Second, the benchmark path is the deck's: US$118/t for FY2027E, falling to the deck's long-run anchor [deck]. The deck's HBA III series is a spot print only with no forecast path, and the high-calorie HBA path of 118.0 USD/t falling to 105.0 USD/t is a different grade, so Newcastle is used only as the escalator while HBA III remains the economic anchor. The result is an implied HBA III in the mid-thirties in every forecast year, which is where the company's own estimate sits: the FY2027E ASP of 21.2 USD/t and the FY2028E ASP of 21.4 USD/t translate back, at the FY2025 realisation, to an HBA III inside the company's own 2026 band of 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t, and the FY2029E ASP of 22.1 USD/t translates to just under the 2025 average of 36.5 USD/t [S8 p.86].

The deck's mid-October HBA III print of 45.5 USD/t is about a quarter above that implied level, and the gap is the largest single piece of conservatism in the valuation. It is disclosed rather than removed, for three reasons that are in the sources. The print is a spot mark, and the card forbids capitalising spot across a life of asset. It has no forward path: holding the October ratio of about thirty-six per cent against the deck's high-calorie path would imply an HBA III path of the low forties falling to the high thirties — roughly a fifth above our implied level in FY2027E, closing to within a tenth by FY2029E — but that is a constructed path, not a sourced one, built on a single month against a full-year 2025 ratio of about a third. And the near-year level is contradicted by the actuals: nine months of revenue of US$55.4m [S17] are already struck at an ASP inside the company's own band, not a quarter higher, so an FY2026E HBA III at the October print is not the most likely path. We keep the path, print both, and say plainly that if the October ratio holds the value is materially higher: that is the largest upside risk to our target, and it is a risk we have chosen not to bank in the base case rather than one we have ignored. The DCF on this anchor is Rp115.

Three items the commodity method card requires are stated explicitly rather than buried. First, the cost-curve position: no public AISC or cash-cost ranking of Indonesian thermal producers is in the archive, so we do not claim a quartile; what we can say is that the 10.64 per tonne nine-month cash cost is the number the equity has to earn against, and it is the single largest sensitivity in the model. Second, NAV at spot: the DCF at our through-cycle deck path gives Rp115 per share; the deck's spot newc of US$150/t is above the highest benchmark column of the sensitivity table, so the same model at spot is higher, not lower. The nearest engine read in this report is the top benchmark column at the base FX row of the sensitivity table — the cell the table prints above the DCF value — and the read at spot is higher again, because the spot price exceeds even that column's benchmark. Third, net debt against trough EBITDA: opening net debt of US$60.7m against FY2026E EBITDA of US$14.7m is 4.1x, a ratio the balance sheet cannot carry through a second trough year, which is why the liquidity risks are ranked as high-impact in the risk section. The three non-operating IUP-OPs are now carried at a sourced value rather than at zero. The previous revision said there was "no separate book value, no sunk capex"; that was wrong. [S12 p.14] prints mining properties and exploration-and-evaluation assets of US$77.5m at 31 December 2025 with no accumulated amortisation shown [S12 Note 11], which is the cumulative sunk acquisition cost of the licence package, and the cash-flow statement shows the acquisition spend that built it [S12 p.20]. The LK does not split the carrying value by licence, so the allocation is by licence count: six IUP-OPs, of which three are operating, so one-third of the balance is attributed to the three non-operating licences and enters the DCF, the multiple and the SOTP equity through the valuation bridge. It is carried at cost, not at a project DCF, because no project cash flow, reserve statement or mine plan for those three is archived, and the operating mines' share is already inside the DCF cash flows and is not added twice. The same allocation applies in the bull, so the bull is no longer an upper bound that excludes a sourced asset. The 91.8 of reserves left in the ground at the end of the thirty-year window remain unvalued — a value life, not a renewable licence, sets the horizon, and no renewal beyond the current applications is archived — and we disclose that option rather than price it.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check uses the peer median, applied to the last audited year's EBITDA restated from the LK — FY2025A, not a metric trailing to the valuation date. The data pack's LTM field carries Yahoo's partial D&A charge — a fraction of the audited charge — so we restate FY2025 revenue from the filing and the engine rebuilds the FY2025A figure on the audited depreciation, giving US$18.0m at the filing's own margin [S12 Note 10, S8 p.12]. The peer median is 5.2, not a blend with IATA's own five-year average: that average spans the aviation-to-coal pivot and the depressed-EBITDA years, so it is not a through-cycle multiple [S0]. The leg produces Rp47, -59.7% below the DCF, because the peer multiple is applied to a single trough year's earnings while the DCF prices the ramp and the normalised cash margin. The card's own cross-checks confirm it is a floor rather than a second valuation: the dividend-capacity anchor is empty because there is no paid stream; and the EV/reserves read of the DCF against 298 Mt of stated reserves is low in absolute terms with no peer series in the archive to rank it. We therefore keep the trough multiple at a minority weight — the DCF 85%, the multiple 15%, down from just under a third — because at the bottom of the cycle a trough-year multiple is the least appropriate anchor and the card's cross-checks do not supply a replacement value. The dividend-yield method carries zero weight because the company pays no dividend [S0, S12].

The valuation bridge adds the full discretionary-fund balance at 30 September 2026, US$18.7m: the Scotts and Regency funds are short-term investments managed on a discretionary basis and marked at fair value through profit or loss, and they sit outside the mining cash flows [S17 Note 13]. We use the 30 September 2026 balance because cash is taken at the same date [F72] [S17]; the June 2026 value was higher and the FY2025 balance lower [S13, S12 Note 13]. Gross debt is the one line still on the 30 June pack figure: the Q3 LK prints debt instrument by instrument rather than as a single total. The seven lines it prints on page five — current and non-current bank loans, lease liabilities, bonds and factoring — sum to a 30 September gross debt a little over one million dollars below the pack's 30 June total, under two percent of net debt and a fraction of a rupee per share in the DCF. We therefore keep the pack's debt total and state the gap rather than imply the two dates are identical; the bridge's net debt is marginally overstated, and correcting it would raise the value by well under one rupee [S17 p.5]. We do not add the reclamation provision because it is small at the balance-sheet date, and we do not add any value for the new controller's intentions because no transaction or plan is archived [S12, S4]. The bridge also carries one negative line: a probability-weighted cost of the rights issue the liquidity gap implies, so that the dilution the previous revision only described in prose sits inside the target instead of beside it. The arithmetic is in the assumptions file; the effect is about four per cent of base value before weighting and about one per cent of the weighted target after it, and the engine cannot do it inside a scenario because its share-count switch is an income-statement line that does not reach per-share value. The post-balance-sheet review is in the assumptions file; the material events are the control change and rename, the controller's 19 October purchase, the Q3 2026 results, the pending RKAB revision, the port/conveyor programme and the 30 September 2026 liquidity position [S4, S5, S8, S16, S17].

The two commodity-card cross-checks are shown here. The dividend-capacity anchor is not a paid yield: the company pays 0.0% and has no dividend record [S0, S12], so the relevant capacity measure is the FY2027E FCFE yield at the current price, 6.1% before any payout [S0]. A normal payout would be a fraction of that, not the high-single-digit yield the market would need to justify the price as an income name. On EV/reserves, the DCF enterprise value of US$213.6m against 298 Mt of stated reserves [F5] is the relevant comparison; at the current price the market's capitalisation plus net debt is close to that enterprise value on the same reserve base [S0], so the reserve cross-check no longer flags the equity as expensive. The IDX coal anchor is normally dividend capacity; IATA does not pay, so the market must be using a price-recovery/volume anchor, which is the bet this report is testing.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest way to state the disagreement, and this revision fixes both of its errors. Scaling the deck's Newcastle path and re-running the model, the price of Rp72 is reached at a benchmark about eight per cent below our FY2027E level; translated at the FY2027E realisation of 18.0% that is an implied ASP below the FY2026E ASP of 20.8 USD/t, and an implied HBA III just under the low end of the company's own 2026 estimate [S0, S8, deck]. The earlier translation was struck at the long-run realisation, which overstated the market-implied price by about a sixth, and it used the engine's own scenario solver, which is not usable here: the scenario mechanism pins every year after the last explicit one at a single value, so a shock to a deck variable flattens the long-run path and destroys value for a reason that has nothing to do with the price. Solved through that route the model prints an implied benchmark close to the deck and makes the market look almost fairly priced; solved on the deck itself, the answer is a discount. We report the clean number, disclose the artefact, and do not use the scenario tails as prices. The conclusion is the opposite of the previous revision's: at Rp72 the market is not assuming a better coal price than the company projects, it is assuming a worse one, and discounting the mining assets to less than half the DCF's value once the non-operating bridge is set aside.

What today's price implies is not absurd in a market that has lost confidence: coal equities can de-rate on a balance sheet, and a new controlling shareholder can change the story in either direction. But the fundamental value is Rp113 and the return to it is 57.1%, so the rating is BUY. The DCF at Rp115 is above the price and the multiple cross-check at Rp47 is below it; the blend lands at our Rp113 target [S0, S12]. The move from the level published on 6 November is now attributed correctly, and it is not one driver. Seven lines account for all of it, and each is an engine run rather than an assertion: the USD risk-free rate the refreshed macro deck carries, up a couple of basis points, which cuts value; the USD/IDR spot the same deck carries, moved from the level the previous revision used, which also cuts value because it translates the dollar cash flows; the one-third allocation of the US$77.5m licence carrying value to the three non-operating IUP-OPs, the largest line and the one that adds a sourced asset the previous revision carried at zero [S12 p.14, Note 11]; the reweighting of the trough EV/EBITDA leg to 15%, which raises the blend because that leg sits below the DCF; the step to the 22.0% statutory tax rate, which cuts it; the probability-weighted rights-issue line, which cuts it; and one day of discounting, because today's engine discounts from today's as-of date while the 6 November figure was struck a day earlier. Those seven lines net to the move from the 6 November blend to today's Rp105; on the target the same changes pass through the roll-forward at the cost of equity to Rp119 and the probability weighting across the three scenarios to Rp113, a weighting that also carries the re-set bull benchmark shock and the removal of the two unsourced per-tonne cost shocks. Both endpoints are printed: the 6 November figures are the published snapshot under the history folder, and the arithmetic, line by line to the rupiah with each line's engine run named and its direction, is in valuation.restatement_bridge in the assumptions file. It is not repeated here because house law keeps typed numbers out of the report; a reader can check every line against that note and reproduce it. The two deck re-marks are the only lines that barely move value: together they take a fraction of a rupiah off the target, with the rupiah about three-quarters of that fraction and the risk-free rate about a quarter, and the previous revision's "only driver of that move is the discount rate" sentence was wrong because it named the discount rate and hid the rupiah. The FX input itself is the deck's, by id, and the deck is the source we cite; the number is not in any onshore article we hold, and the deck's own basis note still describes the reviewed onshore print of 23 October at Rp18,080/USD [S19] while its data field carries a different value. That is an inconsistency in a deck that is not ours to edit; it is disclosed here and in the assumptions file, and the direction of the error is known, because at the onshore print the DCF leg and the target would both be a little higher — a weaker rupiah raises the translation of the dollar cash flows, partly offset by a higher peer multiple. The operating case — volume, price, unit cost and the DCF cash flows — is unchanged apart from the FX translation, and the fuel double-count correction from the previous revision remains in the unit-cost line at 10.64 per tonne in FY2026E [S17, S12 Note 30]. One translation caveat: gross debt is still the 30 June pack figure while equity is translated at the current spot. The rupiah-denominated bonds and facilities are fixed in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah lowers their dollar value — it does not raise it — and the effect is a fraction of a rupiah per share; the Q3 LK prints debt instrument by instrument and the seven lines sum within a million dollars of the pack total, so we disclose the gap rather than restate it [S17 p.5]. The DCF carries 85% of the weight at Rp115; the EV/EBITDA leg carries 15% at Rp47; the blend today is Rp105, rolled forward at the cost of equity to a base case of Rp119 and probability-weighted across the three scenarios to Rp113. The multiple leg is the lower of the two because a peer median applied to one year of earnings cannot see the ramp; it is not a second, more cautious valuation of the same cash flows, and it does not set the view. The previous version struck that leg on the data pack's LTM field, which carried Yahoo's partial D&A charge; restating it to the audited charge lifted the leg and the target [S0, S12, S17]. We would cut the rating on a sourced cost step-up, a volume path that falls short of the plan, a refinancing at a penalty coupon, or a stockpile that cannot be sold at its carried value [S8, S11, S12].

A life-of-asset DCF values the tonnes the company can economically extract, prices them at a through-cycle level and subtracts the capital needed to extract them. It is the right frame for a depleting asset because it does not assume the business lasts forever and it makes the reinvestment requirement explicit. The weakness is that the answer is sensitive to the long-run price and the discount rate, so the analysis is only as good as the sourced price anchor and the cost curve. That is why the report cross-checks the DCF against a multiple and a reverse DCF rather than presenting a single point estimate.

The downside risks are ranked by likelihood and impact. The price is now both the highest-likelihood and the highest-impact risk: a lower low-calorie realisation would compress an already thin cash margin, and the product has no pricing power [S8]. The quota is re-ranked to a 2027 renewal risk rather than the top 2026 risk. Only 2.0 Mt was approved as the initial quota and the revision was still being processed in August [S6, S8, S5], but nine-month revenue of US$55.4m implies sales above that initial quota at every sourced price [S17, F2], so the mid-year revision was delivered for 2026; what is not archived is any commitment that it rolls into 2027, which is why the bear now carries a delivery shortfall rather than a quota cap. The balance-sheet risk is the refinancing of the matured Series B bond at a higher rate or on tighter terms, with cash of US$1.5m at 30 September 2026, factoring liabilities of US$8.1m and current liabilities of US$77.3m above current assets of US$62.1m [S17]. The inventory risk is the US$37.5m stockpile, of which coal is US$26.6m [S17 Note 8]; an NRV writedown or an unsold-tonne/quality problem would hit book equity and the tax shield rather than the cash cost. The reported profit is also exposed to rupiah-dollar translation: the US$2.4m nine-month exchange loss was larger than the entire net profit [S17]. The operational risk is contractor concentration and mine-plan execution at KPP [S11]. The governance risk is the new controlling shareholder's intentions, the low free float, the unresolved special-board status and the undisclosed pledge status [S4, S14, S15]. The fiscal drag is the statutory rate we now carry from FY2026E, which removes the one-year benefit the previous revision spread across five years [S12 Note 2n]. The related-party risk is that US$10.3m of the nine months' funding came from parties connected to the controlling group [S17 p.10], so a withdrawal of that support would leave the company facing its refinancing with US$1.5m of cash. The macro risk is a stronger rupiah or a higher domestic interest-rate path, both of which raise the discount rate and the debt cost.

The bear case now rests on the sourced outcome, not on the stale quota. Volume is held below plan at the company's own historical delivery: 2025 production came in at 80.0% of that year's RKAB target [S3], so the ramp slips rather than collapses; the Series B refinancing fails at a penalty coupon — the bear's cost-of-debt shock is larger than the bull's, because a refinancing failure is not the mirror image of a clean refinancing [S12, S17]; and the low-calorie price fades faster than the quality discount narrows. The old half-volume shock is gone: nine-month revenue already implies sales above the initial approved quota, so it had no basis. The NRV writedown is no longer a per-tonne cash shock either, because an impairment is non-cash: it is carried in the narrative and in the balance-sheet risk above, with the cash effect limited to the tax shield, and the bear's remaining shocks are all cash. In that combination the mining DCF is negative and the bear value of Rp8 is what remains of the non-operating bridge after that shortfall — a trough on the forward path, not a forecast of the reported year, three quarters of which are already actual [S17]. A rights issue is the one branch the engine cannot switch: per-share value divides by the pack's share count, so a share-count shock would not flow through to the value. We therefore carry it as the negative bridge line described in the valuation section — a tenth of the count at a price below value, weighted at the probability of the branch that needs the money — so that it sits inside the Rp113 target and the 57.1% return rather than only in a sentence; at the wider end of the range the cost roughly doubles, and the return falls by another point or so without changing the rating. That is the honest downside: the equity is the residual financier, and the bear should not be modelled as if it were not. The bull case is the filed plan, not a multiple of it: the bull volume shock takes the post-FY2026 years to the company's 7.8 Mt production request, KPP delivers it ahead of schedule, the refinancing clears at the existing coupon, and the low-calorie price holds at the deck's reviewed Newcastle spot rather than reverting to the deck's falling path [S3, F10; S8; S11]. The port/conveyor programme earns no cost benefit in the bull, because the archive discloses the spend but not the uplift [S5]; the previous revision's unsourced per-tonne saving is removed. That is the upper bound of the producing assets plus the non-operating licences at book value; the reserve tail is still carried at zero, so Rp207 does not price it.

The bear case is valued at Rp8 and the bull case at Rp207, with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25% respectively. The base case carries half the probability because it is the most likely path: the company has a signed contractor ramp [S11] and a large reserve base [S8], but the quota renewal and the price are not under its control [S5, S8]. The bear case is not a liquidation scenario; it is the same mine plan at the company's historical delivery rate, a penalty refinancing, an inventory writedown and a lower coal price. The rating is sensitive to the bear weight and we state it plainly: doubling the bear to half the distribution leaves the weighted value about a fifth above the current price, and it takes a bear weight near three-fifths for the value to reach the price at all, so the BUY does not rest on the 25% bear weight. We hold that weight because the bear requires several adverse outcomes at once, none of which is the central case. One mechanical caveat, disclosed because it affects how the tails are read: when a scenario multiplies a deck variable the engine pins every year after the last explicit one at a single value, which flattens the long-run escalation; the bear and the bull are therefore a wider range than a clean re-run would produce, and the reverse DCF in the valuation section is computed on the deck itself rather than through a scenario for that reason.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A published RKAB approval at or above the requested volume would remove the quota overhang. A sustained realised price at or above the HBA III marker would narrow the quality discount. A refinancing at or below the existing coupon and a reduction in the stockpile would remove two of the bear's drivers. Conversely, a materially higher coupon, a missed coupon on the matured tranche, an NRV writedown or a related-party transaction that moves cash out of the listed entity would confirm the bear case. We monitor the monthly HBA III print, the RKAB announcement, the quarterly cash-flow statement, inventory turnover, the factoring balance and the bond trustee notices [S8, S12, S13].

The strongest honest case against our BUY is that the market is capitalising something we cannot see — a dilution larger than the one we quantify, a stockpile that is worth less than its carrying value, or a refinancing on worse terms than the base case — and that the price fell for a reason the archive does not record. A 7.0 Mt producer with a 298 Mt reserve base and a new owner could in principle re-rate, and the stock trades at Rp72 against a year's low of Rp54, below its October monthly mark and the price at which we published the 28 October note, with no archived company disclosure that explains the move [S0]. We checked the candidates: the 19 October stake change was an exercise at a pre-set price, not a signal [S16]; the Q3 results explain the profit fall but not a de-rating of this size [S17]; the special-board list does not change [S14]; and the bond maturity is a known liquidity risk already in our target [S12]. None of those is a company-specific announcement we can source as the cause, and we say so rather than attribute the fall to a 1.1% index move [S18]. Our answer is that optionality is not a source of fundamental value until it is contracted or funded, but the cash flows on the corrected cost line do support a value well above the market price; the return gap is what keeps the rating above HOLD. If the new owner announces a funded expansion, an offtake agreement at a better realised price, a refinancing that removes the liquidity overhang or an asset injection at a fair valuation, we will re-underwrite.

Coal equities can stay expensive for a long time when the market is pricing a change of control or a supply shock, because the narrative is not directly observable in the cash-flow statement. The discipline is to separate the value of the existing assets from the value of the option, and to require a source for the option before putting it in the base case. That is particularly important in Indonesia, where a new controlling shareholder can change the strategy quickly but where the minority shareholder has limited visibility into the plan until it is announced.

Ownership is concentrated and changing. PT Karya Pacific Investama held 62.5% after the 19 October 2026 exercise, up from 48.8% at the end of 2025; the 663.2 million shares were taken at a scheme price of Rp87.0, lifting the stake from 60.4% [S16, S4]. MNC Asia Holding held 18.8% at the end of 2025 and the company states it is no longer part of the MNC group [S4, S12 Note 27]. The two blocks together account for over four-fifths of the shares, so the public float is under one-fifth and the pack's own free-float and insider fields sum to more than the issued capital and cannot both be used [S0, S12 Note 27, S16]. The FY2025 accounts still name MNC Asia Holding as the ultimate parent and Hary Tanoesoedibjo as the ultimate beneficial owner, because the control change was completed after the balance-sheet date; readers should treat the current ownership table as the authoritative one [S12 Note 1, S4]. The new controller's group structure and any pledge of the controlling stake are not disclosed in the archive, so the pledged-share risk cannot be quantified. The stock's special-board status is also unresolved: it entered the special monitoring board in 2024 [S15] and the September 2026 exit list does not include it [S14], so a full-call-auction regime and a residual float under one-fifth remain investability constraints.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and modest in size but structurally important. At FY2025, related-party liabilities were about six per cent of total liabilities, mostly trade payables to PT Karya Pacific Shipping and other group entities, and related-party assets were under one per cent of total assets [S12 Note 26]. There were no related-party revenue transactions disclosed [S12 Note 26]. In the nine months to September 2026 the cash-flow statement shows US$10.3m of new related-party other-payables funding as cash fell to US$1.5m [S17 p.10], which is a related-party liquidity dependence rather than a revenue transaction and is well above the first-half figure the previous revision quoted. The concern is forward-looking: as the controlling group changes, the potential for related-party sales, purchases or asset transfers rises, and the minority has a small float and limited ability to block them. We would treat a large related-party transaction at a non-market price as a governance red flag.

The auditor for FY2025 was KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, with engagement partner Yoyo Sukaryo Djenal and a fee disclosed in the annual report [S8]. The auditor's report is scanned in the archived PDF and the opinion wording could not be text-verified, so we do not assert an unqualified opinion; the accounts were filed with the IDX and the audit report is part of the filing [S12]. The company has no dividend record, so there is no dividend policy to test [S0]. The board and commissioners were changed at the June 2026 AGMS alongside the name change, which is normal after a control transfer but reduces the continuity of oversight [S6].

ESG exposures are typical for Indonesian thermal coal: land use and rehabilitation, water and dust, mine safety, and the long-run demand risk from the energy transition. The company has reclamation provisions and a sustainability report, but the provisions are small relative to the mining footprint, and the archive does not contain a detailed mine-closure cost estimate [S12, S8]. The energy-transition risk is already in the valuation through the long-run price anchor and the declining global demand path; it is not a separate ESG overlay [S8].

Indonesian coal governance is a live investment variable because the controlling family or group can direct related-party transactions, choose the auditor and set the dividend policy. The minority's protections are the listing rules, the independent commissioner and the disclosure regime, not a controlling shareholder's goodwill. A small free float magnifies the effect: a block trade or a margin call on a pledged controlling stake can move the price far more than the fundamental news. That is why the ownership table, the related-party note and the board composition are read alongside the cash-flow statement.

The near-term catalyst calendar is dominated by the balance sheet. The rupiah bond Series B reached its 6 October 2026 maturity, and the archive records neither repayment nor refinancing; the terms will tell us whether the company can fund the ramp without new equity [S12, S17]. The 30 September 2026 stockpile of US$37.5m and the US$8.1m factoring balance are the other near-term monitors: a reduction would ease the liquidity squeeze, while an NRV writedown would confirm the inventory risk [S17]. The ESDM decision on the mid-year RKAB revision is the other near-term event; approval at or above the requested volume would validate the KPP ramp, while a delay would push the volume recovery into 2027 [S8, S5]. The Q3 2026 results are now published: revenue was flat nine-month-on-nine-month but the third quarter's gross profit was below the first half's total but above its per-quarter run-rate, while the exchange loss and finance costs took net profit to US$1.0m [S16, S17]. The next test is the fourth quarter, which carries the year-end shipping and tax true-ups that depressed the FY2025 fourth-quarter result.

The medium-term catalysts are the first full year of the KPP contract and the port/conveyor programme. If KPP delivers the long-run run-rate in 2027 and the port works reduce the shipping bottleneck, the volume and cost lines could beat our base case [S11, S5]. A dividend initiation is not in our forecast and there is no policy to support it, but a sustained free-cash-flow improvement would make it possible; we would treat the first dividend as a signal rather than a base-case assumption [S0, S12].

The KPIs we watch between updates are: the monthly HBA III print and the ICI-5 index; the quarterly sales volume and realised ASP; the cash cost per tonne and the shipping cost per tonne; capex and the port/conveyor spend; net debt and the refinancing of the matured bond; the RKAB approval and any quota revision; and the special-board and free-float status [S8, S12, S14]. Each of these is a line in the model, so a change in any one of them flows straight into the target rather than sitting in a qualitative note.

bear.narrative: The 2027 RKAB cycle does not roll the mid-year revision forward and the company delivers only its historical share of the plan (2025 production was about 80% of the RKAB target [S3]), so the 6.5 Mt ramp slips to about 5.2 Mt; the Series B refinancing fails at a penalty coupon; the low-calorie price fades faster than the quality discount narrows.
